newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Georgia diplomat tried to leave country.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Georgia diplomat tried to leave country.

text.p: A Georgian diplomat alleged to have caused a Washington car crash that killed a teenage girl sought to leave the United States on Thursday but is now back in the U.S. capital, U.S. officials said on Friday.

They said Gueorgui Makharadze, 35, set off by car for New York to catch an outbound flight but returned to Washington after U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher voiced concern that his departure would violate a Georgian government pledge.

The officials disclosed the incident as the United States hailed as courageous Friday's announcement by Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze that he was prepared to lift Makharadze's diplomatic immunity so he can face charges.

The U.S. attorney's office said on Wednesday it believed it had sufficient evidence to prosecute Makharadze over last Friday's five-car smash that killed Joviane Waltrick, a 16-year-old Brazilian girl living in Kensington, Maryland.

It has not yet brought formal charges. But if diplomatic immunity is waived, prosecutors in the attorney's office plan to move fast and present evidence to a grand jury for a possible indictment, federal law enforcement officials said.

The State Department said Shevardnadze's statement did not in itself amount to lifting the immunity and Georgia would have to decide whether to do so if U.S. authorities brought charges against Makharadze.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said that Thursday afternoon Christopher received "some indications that Mr Makharadze was in a car heading for New York City, and we know that there are certain flights that leave JFK (airport) for Frankfurt and Moscow, and that's how you get to Tbilisi."
Christopher then requested that Georgian ambassador Tedo Djaparidze should be called in to the State Department and told that Makharadze should stay in the country, Burns said.

He said he believed the Georgian embassy called Makharadze back to Washington after hearing of Christopher's concern that Georgia honour a previous pledge to keep the diplomat in the United States until investigations were completed.

Although the Georgian government told the U.S. embassy in Tbilisi on Thursday that it planned to recall Makharadze, Shevardnadze changed tack on Friday after an appeal by Christopher to waive the diplomat's immunity.

A Georgian statement said Shevardnadze "is prepared to waive the diplomatic immunity" of Makharadze, who "shall remain in the United States of America until the completion of the investigation and legal procedures unless a different agreement between the two governments is reached."
Burns told reporters: "The United States very much welcomes this step by chairman Shevardnadze."
"It's a courageous step. It's highly unusual in modern diplomacy to see a head of state take such a responsible and courageous position," he said.
U.S. law enforcement officials said action could occur within a week and possible charges included negligent homicide, second-degree murder or involuntary manslaughter, depending on the evidence.

Although Shevardnadze's statement did not itself waive immunity, White House press secretary Mike McCurry said the United States saw it as a commitment to do so if charges are filed. "The statement is clear to that effect," he said.
McCurry said the statement left open the prospect of further diplomatic contact between the two governments. But another U.S. official said: "Our firm view is that there shouldn't be any deal here."
The Georgian embassy said later that Shevardnadze had acted "in the interest of U.S.-Georgian relations and on moral and ethical grounds".

The original decision to recall Makharadze followed "the nearly universal practice" of other countries including the United States, which had refused to waive immunity in criminal cases in recent years in Britain and Russia, it said.
